claims.text: The starting material is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3.
The starting alloy has a homogeneous, fine-grained fcc matrix.
The starting alloy has notable strength and fatigue resistance.
Elevated-temperature degradation is governed by formation and eventual destabilization of a mixed oxide scale.
The mixed oxide scale forms preferentially through oxidation of Cr and Ti.
The initial scale is thin and partially protective and consists mainly of Cr and Ti oxides with minor Al and Fe contributions.
Scale growth stresses and thermal-expansion mismatch cause spallation under oxidizing conditions.
Spallation exposes fresh alloy and thereby promotes renewed rapid oxidation.
Reducing atmospheres transform, dissolve, or reduce the oxide scale and prevent formation of a stable protective barrier.
Loss of the protective scale in reducing atmospheres accelerates continued surface or internal degradation.
The underlying fcc matrix remains largely intact during early exposure despite surface degradation.
Oxidizing exposure will produce periods of apparent mass-gain stabilization interrupted by abrupt increases attributed to scale spallation.
Oxidizing exposure will produce observable oxide-scale cracking or delamination in SEM/EDS analyses.
Reducing exposure will produce less continuous scaling but more evidence of subsurface oxidation and near-surface microstructural change.
Fatigue properties may eventually degrade during prolonged exposure.
The proposed scale-controlled mechanism is expected to dominate above approximately 600 °C during prolonged exposures.
Increasing Al or Cr sufficiently to stabilize continuous Al2O3 or Cr2O3 would change the degradation pathway.
A controlled comparison at 600, 750, and 900 °C for 25, 50, and 100 hours in oxygen-rich and hydrogen-rich gases can test the proposed mechanism.
Absence of a distinct unstable mixed scale, or observation of an adherent protective scale with no meaningful atmosphere-dependent degradation, would falsify the proposed scale-instability mechanism.

contradictions.description: The mechanism describes spallation as removal of oxide, whereas the predicted outcome attributes abrupt mass increases directly to spallation. Direct scale loss would ordinarily cause a mass decrease; renewed oxidation after exposure of fresh metal could cause a subsequent increase, but that sequence is not stated.
